papers.title_in_file: Precise Photon Arrival Time Measurement via Time to Frequency Demultiplexing
papers.version_note: arXiv:2606.15030v1, 13 Jun 2026; text layer matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper that maps photon arrival time to wavelength channels with multiplexed sum-frequency conversion in a multi-period PPLN waveguide and estimates arrival time from channel count ratios, with RMSE of about 0.6 to 1 ps in a three-channel test.

assertions.value: The authors state that they demonstrate a nonlinear-optics approach that translates the temporal information of single photons to a wavelength distribution by frequency conversion, followed by de-multiplexed detection, using a multi-color, pulse-delayed pump laser to drive multiplexed frequency conversion.
quotes: We demonstrate a nonlinear-optics approach to precise measurement of photon arrival time, by translating the temporal information of single photons to a wavelength distribution of frequency conversion followed by de-multiplexed detection.
It uses a multi-color, pulse-delayed pump laser to drive multiplexed frequency conversion, transducing photons to various frequency channels according to their arrival time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's own method and scope.

assertions.value: The authors claim in the abstract that, by photon detection in each channel, the measurement resolution and accuracy can reach picosecond level, much lower than the detectors' naive resolution and significantly beating the shot-noise limited direct detection.
quotes: By photon detection in each channel, the measurement resolution and accuracy can reach picosecond level, much lower than the detectors’ naive resolution and significantly beating the shot-noise limited direct detection.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison to direct detection in the body (Fig. 7) is against a computed formula, not a measured direct-detection run, and the experiment used three channels with a roughly 12.5 ps pump (Section 4), so 'picosecond level' is the measured RMSE of about 1 ps, not a pulse-width-limited figure.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that the approach supports event-ready operations, capable of detecting randomly arriving single photons with no dead window. The conclusion states more weakly that it largely mitigates the dead time associated with repetitive temporal scanning.
quotes: our approach supports event-ready operations, capable of detecting randomly arriving single photons with no dead window.
Also, it largely mitigates the dead time associated with repetitive temporal scanning and is suitable for photons that arrive randomly or only once.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says no dead window; the conclusion says largely mitigates. The reported experiments held the delay fixed per integration window and scanned it between windows, so the event-ready, single-photon property is argued, not run as a random-arrival test.

assertions.value: The authors state two requirements for the system: low background noise, with injected noise comparable to or lower than the detector dark counts, and single-shot operation, able to determine a random photon arrival time without repetitive or adaptive measurements.
quotes: Low background noise, where the injected noise is comparable to or lower than the detector dark counts;
Single-shot operation, where the system is capable of precisely determining a random photon arrival time without relying on repetitive or adaptive measurements.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 states the design goals as the paper's own scope.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no measured background or dark-count figure against the first requirement.

assertions.value: The authors describe a multiplexed quantum frequency converter (m-QFC) pumped by multiple pulse trains, each of a different color, to convert the signal into different wavelengths by sum- or difference-frequency generation; all pulse trains share the same period but are relatively delayed.
quotes: The m-QFC is pumped by multiple pulse trains, each of a different color, to convert the signal into different wavelengths through the generation of sum- or difference-frequency.
All pulse trains share the same period, but are relatively delayed with respect to one another.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 states the architecture of the paper's own method.

assertions.value: The authors state that the detectors provide the coarse photon arrival time, limited by their timing jitter, while the identity of the detector that clicks provides the fine timing information, determined by the pump pulse width.
quotes: the detectors provide the coarse photon arrival time, limited by their timing jitter, while the identity of the detector that clicks provides the fine timing information, determined by the pump pulse width.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiment in Section 4 does not use the coarse detector time tags (Section 4, p.10); only the fine, wavelength-channel part is tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pulse trains can be generated with frequency-comb lines, each train formed by a subset of comb lines; the period is set by the comb-line spacing and the pulse width by the spectral width of the subset.
quotes: Such pulse trains can be generated with frequency-comb lines, where each train is formed by a subset of comb lines.
The period is determined by the comb-line spacing, whereas the pulse width is determined by the spectral width of the subset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 states how the paper's pulse trains are made.

assertions.value: The authors give a practical design example: a PPLN waveguide with 10 quasi-phase-matching peaks, ten pulse trains carved from comb lines with 25-GHz spacing, pulses of about 4 ps, and Si-APD detectors with typical timing jitter of about 40 ps FWHM, so that the which-detector information gives a fine resolution of 4 ps.
quotes: In a practical example, the m-QFC can consist of a PPLN waveguide with 10 quasi-phase-matching peaks [26].
Ten pulse trains are carved out of a laser beam of comb lines with 25-GHz spacing; see Fig. 1(a). Each pulse is about 4 ps long
The timing jitter of commercially available Si-APD detectors is typically about 40 ps FWHM.
The which-detector information, on the other hand, gives a fine resolution of 4 ps.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a proposed design, not the tested one. The experiment used three channels and a pump pulse of about 12.5 ps (Section 4). A 25 GHz spacing implies a 40 ps period (inference; the paper does not state it).

assertions.value: The authors use a ratio-manifold estimator: the measured channel counts are normalized to a ratio vector and compared with a calibrated delay-dependent reference; the arrival-time estimate is the delay in the calibration set that minimizes a distance function between the calibrated and measured ratio vectors.
quotes: Here, we use a ratio-manifold estimator that compares the measured spectral count distribution with a calibrated delay-dependent reference.
The arrival time is estimated by comparing rmeas with the calibrated manifold over the delay set T .
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the estimator the results depend on.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints Eq. 4 garbled; it reads as the squared Euclidean (L2) norm of R(tau) minus r_meas, and Eq. 5 as the argmin over the delay set.

assertions.value: The authors state that the normalization suppresses common-mode power fluctuations and channel-independent throughput variations while preserving the relative inter-channel pattern that encodes the timing information.
quotes: This normalization suppresses common-mode power fluctuations and channel-independent throughput variations, while preserving the relative inter-channel pattern that encodes the timing information.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing a textbook reference (62), that in the high-count regime the ratio mapping approaches a deterministic manifold, whereas at low photon number the estimation uncertainty is governed by shot-noise fluctuations in the underlying counts.
quotes: In the high-count regime, the ratio mapping approaches a deterministic manifold, whereas at low photon number, the estimation uncertainty is governed by shot-noise fluctuations in the underlying counts [62].

assertions.value: The authors claim that, because the estimator operates entirely in calibrated ratio space, sub-picosecond reporting can be achieved by evaluating the manifold on a finer delay grid without modifying the physical hardware.
quotes: sub-picosecond reporting can be achieved by evaluating the manifold on a finer delay grid without modifying the physical hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 4 shows the finer grid needs more photons: the 0.5 ms fine-grid RMSE is worse than the coarse-grid one.

assertions.value: The authors state that the estimator is perhaps the simplest method to find the arrival time, shown for illustration, and that more sophisticated methods, including machine learning, could give even higher resolution and/or accuracy.
quotes: It is worth noting that this estimator is perhaps the simplest method to find the arrival time, for illustration purpose.
More sophisticated methods, including those of machine learning, could give even higher resolution and/or accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that the estimator does not use any time-tag information from the detectors, and that a better data processing method will be a subject of future studies; they say the time-tag information can be finer than the pump-pulse-width information at high photon counts.
quotes: Also, it does not utilize any time-tag information from the detectors.
A better data processing method can improve the system performance and will be a subject of future studies.
The electronic time tags recorded by the detectors are not included in the ratio-based estimator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Section 2 and again in Section 4 as a scope limit of the reported results.
assertions.reader_inference: Stated in Section 2 and again in Section 4 as a scope limit of the reported results.

assertions.value: The authors generate a 25 GHz line-spacing comb with an optical frequency comb generator driven by a 25 GHz RF signal, and shape pump and signal lines with a 10 GHz resolution wave-shaper (Finisar 16000A) that performs line-by-line amplitude and phase control.
quotes: driven by a 25 GHz RF signal, producing a broadband comb with 25 GHz line spacing.
The remaining power is directed to a 10 GHz resolution wave-shaper (Finisar 16000A), which performs line-by-line amplitude and phase control to synthesize the pump and signal wavelengths.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 describes the paper's own apparatus.

assertions.value: The authors control the relative delay between pump and signal pulses with an optical delay line in the signal arm, and add 10 m of single-mode fiber in the pump arm to introduce controlled chromatic dispersion and relative timing offsets between comb lines.
quotes: An optical delay line in the signal arm controls the relative delay
The pump arm includes 10 m single-mode fiber to introduce controlled chromatic dispersion and generate relative timing offsets between comb lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 describes the paper's own apparatus.
assertions.reader_inference: The delay is set by a mechanical delay line between measurements, so the test does not exercise random arrival of single photons.

assertions.value: The authors separate the visible outputs with a free-space grating spectrograph into three spatial paths, each filtered by cascaded 1 nm band-pass filters, and detect photons with three Si-APDs recorded by a synchronized time-tagging unit.
quotes: Steering mirrors direct the dispersed beams into three spatial paths, each coupled to a fiber collimator and filtered using cascaded 1 nm band-pass filters for spectral isolation.
Photon arrival events are detected using three Si-APDs and recorded using a synchronized time-tagging unit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 describes the paper's own apparatus.
assertions.reader_inference: Three channels were demonstrated, against ten in the design example.

assertions.value: The authors state that channel-dependent throughput variations from coupling and filtering are compensated in post-processing by using normalized photon-count ratios instead of absolute count rates.
quotes: Channel-dependent throughput variations arising from coupling and filtering are compensated in post-processing through the use of normalized photon-count ratios rather than absolute count rates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states how the paper handles throughput differences.

assertions.value: The authors report that waveguide characterization at 39.4 ± 0.1 degrees C reveals three distinct second harmonic generation phase-matching peaks at 1552.7 nm, 1555.2 nm and 1557.7 nm, each corresponding to one of three poling periods.
quotes: Waveguide characterization at 39.4 ± 0.1◦C reveals three distinct second harmonic generation (SHG) phase-matching peaks at 1552.7 nm, 1555.2 nm, and 1557.7 nm, each corresponding to the three poling periods.
assertions.reader_inference: The ◦ in the quote is the text layer's degree sign.

assertions.value: The authors use a fixed telecom-band signal at 1560.666 nm with pump wavelengths of 1544.775 nm, 1549.575 nm and 1554.385 nm, producing visible outputs at 776.34 nm, 777.55 nm and 778.76 nm respectively.
quotes: For timing measurements, a fixed telecom-band signal at 1560.666 nm interacts with pump wavelengths of (1544.775 nm, 1549.575 nm, and 1554.385 nm), producing spectrally separated visible outputs at 776.34 nm, 777.55 nm, and 778.76 nm, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the operating wavelengths of the paper's own run.

assertions.value: The authors report intensity FWHM pulse widths of approximately 3.8 ps for the signal and 12.5 ps for the pump.
quotes: The signal and pump pulses have intensity full width at half maximum (FWHM) pulse widths of approximately 3.8 ps and 12.5 ps, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the pulse widths of the paper's own run.
assertions.reader_inference: The pump pulse is about three times wider than the roughly 4 ps pulse of the design example in Section 2, and the reported RMSE (about 0.6 to 1 ps) is far below the 12.5 ps pump width; the paper does not explain this beyond the ratio-based interpolation.

assertions.value: The authors report that each channel shows a distinct temporal response peak reflecting the channel-dependent pump-signal overlap in the multi-period PPLN waveguide, measured at integration times of 100 ms and 5 ms, and that the same peak structure is preserved at the shorter integration time.
quotes: Each channel exhibits a distinct temporal response peak, reflecting the channel-dependent pump–signal overlap inside the multi-period PPLN waveguide.
for integration times of 100 ms and 5 ms.
the same peak structure is preserved

assertions.value: The authors state that the experimental delay scan covered 20 to 60 ps, displayed shifted to a window of 0 to 40 ps within a period of comb lines.
quotes: mapping the experimental scan range of 20–60 ps to the displayed window of 0–40 ps within a period of comb lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the delay range of the reported tests.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported estimates therefore resolve arrival time only within one 40 ps window, which matches the 25 GHz comb period (inference).

assertions.value: The authors report that, for a representative measurement, the minimum of the distance function correctly recovered the applied delay on the 1 ps calibration grid.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, p.7; Fig. 5(a,b), 100 ms integration time
quotes: correctly recovering the applied delay on the 1 ps grid.
assertions.reader_inference: Fig. 5(b) caption: true delay 21.000 ps, estimate 21.000 ps (single representative point).

assertions.value: The authors state that the fine-grid distance curve retains a clear minimum, showing that sub-picosecond retrieval is possible when the photon counts are sufficient to resolve the closely spaced calibration points.
quotes: Nevertheless, the distance curve shown in Fig. 5(d), retains a clear minimum, showing that sub-picosecond retrieval is possible when the photon counts are sufficient to resolve the closely spaced calibration points.
assertions.reader_inference: Fig. 5(d) caption: true 15.300 ps, estimate 15.100 ps, a single representative point with a 0.2 ps error.

assertions.value: The authors state that a finer calibration grid reduces the error from coarse sampling but puts neighboring calibration points closer in ratio space, so the finer grid is more sensitive to photon-counting noise under low-count conditions.
quotes: However, neighboring (0.1 ps) calibration points are closer together in ratio space, making them harder to distinguish when photon-counting noise is present.
Therefore, the finer grid is more sensitive to photon-counting noise under low-count conditions.

assertions.value: The authors quantify retrieval error as the root-mean-square error between estimated and true arrival times over the evaluated delay points, and state that this metric measures how accurately the calibrated wavelength-channel ratio vector recovers the arrival time.
quotes: The retrieval error is quantified by the root-mean-square error
is the number of evaluated delay points.
This metric directly measures how accurately the calibrated wavelength-channel ratio vector recovers the photon arrival time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 defines the metric the results depend on.
assertions.reader_inference: The RMSE formula is garbled in the text layer; the value restates its prose.

assertions.value: The authors report an RMSE of 1.02 ps over the evaluated timing window with the 1 ps calibration grid at an integration time of 5 ms.
quotes: int = 5 ms, as shown in Fig. 6(a), the estimated photon arrival times closely follow the ideal diagonal, giving an RMSE of 1.02 ps
assertions.reader_inference: The calibration grid step is 1 ps, so an RMSE of 1.02 ps is close to the grid step itself; the paper does not separate grid error from noise at this setting.

assertions.value: The authors report RMSE values of 2.29 ps, 1.41 ps and 1.22 ps with the 1 ps calibration grid for integration times of 0.5 ms, 1 ms and 2 ms respectively.
quotes: The RMSE values are 2.29 ps, 1.41 ps, and 1.22 ps for
int = 0.5 ms, 1 ms, and 2 ms, respectively.

assertions.value: The authors report an RMSE of 0.57 ps with the 0.1 ps calibration grid over a zoomed timing interval at an integration time of 5 ms, and state that this shows the channel ratios carry arrival-time information below the 1 ps coarse-grid spacing and beyond the naive timing resolution of the detector and TDC chain.
quotes: int = 5 ms, the photon-count ratios are stable enough to support this finer search, and the retrieved timing remains close to the ideal diagonal with an RMSE of 0.57 ps
neighboring (0.1 ps) calibration points are closer together in ratio space

wavelength-channel photon count ratios carry arrival-time information below the 1 ps coarse-grid spacing and beyond the naive timing resolution of the detector and time-to-digital converter (TDC) chain.
assertions.reader_inference: The 0.57 ps figure is over a zoomed interval (about 13 to 19 ps in Fig. 6), not the full window.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the 0.1 ps calibration grid the RMSE is 3.20 ps at the shortest integration time of 0.5 ms, and improves to 0.89 ps and 0.62 ps at 1 ms and 2 ms respectively.
quotes: neighboring (0.1 ps) calibration points are closer together in ratio space
where the shortest integration time of 0.5 ms, gives an RMSE of 3.20 ps.
As the integration time increases to 1 ms and 2 ms, more photons are collected, the ratio fluctuations are reduced, and the RMSE improves to 0.89 ps and 0.62 ps, respectively.
assertions.reader_inference: At 0.5 ms the fine grid (3.20 ps) is worse than the coarse grid (2.29 ps).

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the retrieval error is strongly influenced by photon-counting noise in the ratio measurement rather than by instability of the nonlinear conversion process.
quotes: The improvement with increasing integration time indicates that the retrieval error is strongly influenced by photon-counting noise in the ratio measurement rather than by instability of the nonlinear conversion process.
assertions.reader_inference: No separate stability measurement of the conversion process is reported.

assertions.value: The authors define the direct-detection reference as the timing precision from the independently measured RMS jitter of the detector-TDC chain divided by the square root of the net signal photon number after background subtraction; they call it the conventional timestamp-averaging limit.
quotes: where ������det+TDC is the RMS timing jitter of the detector–TDC chain and ������sig (������int) is the net signal photon number after background subtraction.
This expression represents the conventional timestamp-averaging limit, where the timing uncertainty improves as
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 defines the benchmark the comparison depends on.
assertions.reader_inference: The reference is a computed formula, not a measured direct-detection run. The formula is garbled in the text layer; 'divided by the square root' is read from the printed 1/sqrt form.

assertions.value: The authors report a detector-TDC RMS timing jitter of about 38.117 ps, measured with a trigger-referenced timing histogram using the Si-APD and Swabian time-tagger electronics used in the experiment.
quotes: The measurement was performed with the Si-APD detector and Swabian time-tagger electronics used in the experiment.
Using this procedure, the measured detector–TDC RMS timing jitter is
assertions.reader_inference: RMS jitter here is not directly comparable to the roughly 40 ps FWHM typical figure quoted in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the photon-starved regime, where only a few to tens of photons are detected per integration window, the measured RMSE of the estimator remains below the direct-detection reference over the plotted low-count range, and conclude that time-to-frequency mapping can give a timing advantage when the photon number is too small for effective timestamp averaging.
quotes: where only a few to tens of photons are detected within each integration window.
As a result, the measured RMSE of the proposed estimator remains below the direct-detection reference over the plotted low-count range.
This confirms that time-to-frequency mapping can provide a timing advantage when the photon number is too small for effective timestamp averaging.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against a computed 1/sqrt(N) timestamp-averaging bound, not an estimator that also uses the time tags jointly with the channel ratios. The windows hold several photons each from a fixed delay, so this is not a one-photon-at-a-time test.

assertions.value: The authors state that at larger photon numbers both the estimator and the direct-detection reference improve as more photons are collected, and that the remaining error of the estimator is likely set by calibration-grid spacing, photon-counting noise, residual background, channel imbalance and calibration mismatch.
quotes: both the proposed estimator and the direct-detection reference improve as more photons are collected.
The remaining error of the proposed estimator is likely set by a combination of calibration-grid spacing, photon-counting noise, residual background, channel imbalance, and calibration mismatch.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their current results show picosecond-scale timing estimation with a few detected photon counts, with a clear advantage over a conventional direct-detection reference in the photon-starved regime.
quotes: Our current results show picosecond-scale timing estimation with a few detected photon counts.

assertions.value: The authors state that with improved detection efficiency, larger channel counts, and processing that combines wavelength-channel ratios with detector time-tag information, the approach can be extended toward sub-picosecond timing precision.
quotes: With improved detection efficiency, larger channel counts, and data processing that combines both wavelength-channel ratios and detector time-tag information, this approach can be extended toward sub-picosecond timing precision.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no detection efficiency, conversion efficiency or background count rate, so how far these improvements are from the current setup is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that earlier optical-gating upconversion approaches require an optical delay line to sweep the pump pulses to capture the signal, so are inherently slow and do not support event-ready detection.
quotes: However, these approaches require an optical delay line to sweep the pump pulses to capture the signal [18, 22, 23].
Hence, they are inherently slow and do not support event-ready detection, where a transient signal may arrive at an arbitrary and unknown time.

assertions.value: The authors state that multiplexed frequency conversion was demonstrated previously (reference 24) and that the unique single-shot capability introduced here is new.
quotes: Although multiplexed frequency conversion has been demonstrated previously [24], the unique single-shot capability introduced here is new

assertions.value: The authors state that a single converter with multiple simultaneous phase-matching conditions is more efficient than passing the signal through multiple converters because it minimizes insertion loss.
quotes: The single-device approach is more efficient because it minimizes insertion loss.

assertions.value: The authors state that key applications include remote sensing, such as satellite or airborne single-photon LiDAR for Earth observation, target tracking and photon-efficient ranging, and space-based quantum optical communications.
quotes: Key applications include remote sensing, such as satellite or airborne single-photon LiDAR for Earth observation, target tracking, and photon-efficient ranging
